title: Teach Boys to Leap from Grade 4 to Grade 7
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles answers a new subscriber's question about moving middle prior attaining boys from grades 4 and 5 into 6 and 7, using a video script drawn from 34 years of teaching English. His central claim is that boys respond to transparent numerical targets, speed, public comparison and status, while girls tend to work hard whatever the teacher does. He recommends counting everything, halving the time limits teachers instinctively set, and narrating the room by calling out line counts as he circulates. Effort is then gamified through personal bests and a league table kept in a spreadsheet, with symbolic rewards such as a single Smartie. For quality he leans on Rosenshine's 80 percent success rate, reached through model answers, reconstruction from key words and repeated cloze versions of an essay. His most contrarian point is that scaffolding up to a model slows learning, so teachers should start with the model and scaffold away from it.
points: Numerical targets for lines, sentences or accuracy make expectations transparent and achievable, which Salles says suits boys who want things to be crystal clear.
Setting time limits at half of what teachers think is needed, then extending slightly, forces concentration and can turn an eight-minute task into about two and a half minutes.
Narrating the room and publishing personal bests as league tables turns effort into status, which Salles argues motivates boys more than pleasing the teacher.
An 80 percent success rate by the end of the lesson is built through models, reconstruction from key words and cloze passes that let a student internalise a whole essay.
Starting from the finished model and scaffolding away from it keeps students aware of what excellent looks like, unlike small steps that hide the whole until too late.
quotes: Girls want social learning; they want to be part of a team. This is one of the reasons that they do so well at school. They are people pleasers.

In my experience, teachers spend twice as long on each task as they actually need to. So get yourself a timer, set half the time limit that you think students can do it in, and I guarantee they’ll do it in that half a time limit.
They know two things: they will be exposed with a low number again, and they will lose status.
Boys are much more likely to want status by being better than their friends. And how do they achieve status? They write more, they write quicker, and they get higher point scores.
I used to reward kids with a single Smartie. You know, “The top three in this next activity are going to get a whole Smartie each.” It was largely symbolic.
Now, another thing that all students need is an 80% success rate. This is something that Rosenshine tells us, and it’s not 80% all the way through the lesson
So if we teach from the model and scaffold away from the model once they’ve seen it, we have dramatically more success than if we scaffold up to the model.
